name: Yawalapiti
confidence_why: Mujica (1992) and Tapi Yawalapíti (2021), two independent first-hand descriptions thirty years apart, both give minimal pairs such as íʃa 'canoe' versus iʃá 'blood' showing that stress falls unpredictably on the final or penultimate syllable, and the only hedges are Tapi's unsupported 'pitch accent' label and a quoted personal communication from Couto that phrase-level stress shifts may be intonational.

new_statements.quote: Ywalapíti é uma língua de pitch-accent. Há um conjunto de pares de palavras que contrastam quanto ao acento, como entre as palavras para ‘canoa’ e ‘sangue’: íʃa ‘canoa’ / iʃá ‘sangue’. Estes dados sugerem que Yawalapíti possui acento fonológico. Não se pode dizer que o acento do Yawalapíti é previsível, por várias palavras insegmentáveis morfologicamente terem o acento na penúltima sílaba e outas palavras da mesma natureza terem o acento na última sílaba [...] Um fato a ser destacado no âmbito do acento em Yawalapíti é o de que, operações morfológicas provocam o deslocamento de acento para a direita ou para a esquerda.
new_statements.translation: Yawalapíti is a pitch-accent language. There is a set of word pairs that contrast in accent, such as the words for 'canoe' and 'blood': íʃa 'canoe' / iʃá 'blood'. These data suggest that Yawalapíti has phonological accent. One cannot say that Yawalapíti accent is predictable, because several morphologically unsegmentable words have the accent on the penultimate syllable and other words of the same nature have the accent on the last syllable [...] A fact to be highlighted regarding accent in Yawalapíti is that morphological operations cause the accent to shift to the right or to the left.
new_statements.citation: Yawalapíti, Tapi. 2021. Documentação e descrição da língua yawalapíti (aruák): uma língua que não deve morrer. MA dissertation, Universidade de Brasília. 211 pp.
new_statements.locator: Chapter II 'Fonologia segmental e aspectos prosódicos', section 2.8 ACENTO, pp. 91-93 (printed page = PDF page)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 211 pp., printed page = PDF page (p.91 carries printed '91'). Section 2.8 ACENTO runs pp. 91-93. Every sentence of the quotation is on pp. 91-92 exactly as given, including the typo 'outas'; the compiler '/' and '[..]' are only splice markers between the minimal pair and around the elided example lists. I re-rendered pp. 91-92 to PNG (text drops the IPA stress marks) and confirmed the placements the compiler lists: penult ['ma:pa] 'abelha', ['hiɾi] 'cipó', ['wiɲɨ] 'rio', [pi'tipɨ] 'bem-te-vi', [ma'waɾi] 'cobra cipó', [ma'jaku] 'cesto'; final [ʧĩ'ʧa] 'corda', [tua'ɾi], [ija'ka] 'jacaré', [ɨ'pɨ] 'hoje', [a'ka] 'pequi', [jana'pa], [ma'lu], [ma'pi], [ka'pa], [iʂɨ'pɨ], [itʃu'na] 'timbó'; affix s…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog entry for Yawalapiti has an empty rule field and there are no existing statements; this dissertation supplies the first placement statement: contrastive, unpredictable accent between penult and final syllable on roots, mobile under affixation and phrase position, labelled 'pitch accent' by the author.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent is contrastive (minimal pair íʃa 'canoe' vs iʃá 'blood') and not predictable: unsegmentable roots fall on the penult (['ma:pa] 'bee', ['hiɾi] 'vine', [pi'tipɨ] 'bem-te-vi', [ma'waɾi] 'vine snake', [ma'jaku] 'basket') or on the final syllable ([tʃĩ'tʃa] 'rope', [ija'ka] 'caiman', [a'ka] 'pequi', [ma'lu] 'false', [ma'pi] 'skin', [itʃu'na] 'timbó'). Affixation shifts the accent left or right (['patʃa] 'eats', ['patʃatsa] 'must eat', [pa'tʃapa] 'you are eating', [patʃu'ka] 'you may eat'), and the accent of a word also moves with its position in the utterance (utterance-initial ['iʂa] vs utterance-final [i'ʂa] 'canoe'). The author labels the system 'pitch accent' but gives no acoustic evidence and says on p. 98 that the acoustic study of accent was left for later work.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Secondary-stress marks appear in some transcriptions on p. 91-92 (e.g. [ˌhiakutuˈka] 'may leave', [ˌhiaˈwatʃĩ] 'likes', [ˌwiʎɨˈtʃĩ] 'itch'), always on an initial syllable two or more syllables before the main accent, but the text does not comment on them.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent shifts under morphological operations (to the left or the right) and under position in the utterance; Fábio Pereira Couto (personal communication, quoted p. 93) suggests the latter shift may be a matter of sentence-level accent (rising-falling intonation contour) 'descartando, por exemplo, o acento lexical' (setting aside the lexical accent). The dissertation also notes (p. 30) that Mitzila Mujica's 1992 UnB thesis on Yawalapíti contains 'algumas observações sobre duração e acento' (some observations on length and accent); that work is not in the open list.
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Yawalapíti as spoken in the Xingu Indigenous Park (Mato Grosso, Brazil) by a native-speaker author; no dialect split is mentioned. The 1992 Mujica thesis (not opened, not in the open list) is cited as containing observations on length and accent.

readall_conflicts: Only one work was open, so there is no cross-source disagreement. Within the work there is a tension: the opening sentence calls Yawalapíti a 'pitch accent' language, while the rest of section 2.8 describes it as ordinary contrastive word stress (a minimal pair, penult vs final placement on unsegmentable roots, shifts under affixation) with no pitch-track or acoustic evidence, and the author states on p. 98 that the acoustic study of accent was not carried out in the dissertation. A further hedge is Couto's quoted personal communication (p. 93) that the phrase-position shift may reflect sentence intonation rather than lexical accent, which, if taken to its conclusion, would question whether there is lexical accent at all; the author nonetheless keeps the claim of phonological accent.

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the Mujica 1992 PDF we hold at every stated locator (pp.31, 44-45, 46, 76). Mujica 1992 is a first-hand phonological description with minimal pairs and was the only such work until Tapi Yawalapíti 2021, which I downloaded from the UnB repository; its sec. 2.8 (pp.91-93) states stress is phonological and not predictable (penult vs final on unsegmentable words, minimal pair íʃa/iʃá), i.e. it confirms classification lexical, edge=right. Refinements worth noting in the record but not changing the classification: Tapi calls the language 'pitch accent', reports stress displacement under affixation (including one antepenult-stressed suffixed verb form) and under utterance position, and says no acoustic study has yet been done. The remaining Glottolog items are an unpublished 1991 conference paper by the same author and an unpublished morphology study (França 2011, per Tapi 202

sources.note: Only description newer than our 1992 deciding source; native-speaker author; sec. 2.8 independently confirms contrastive (unpredictable penult vs final) stress on monomorphemic words and adds morphological and phrase-position stress shifts (one suffixed form [ˈpatʃatsa] shows stress left of the penult, qualifying Mujica's strict two-syllable window for complex words). Should be added as a corroborating source.
